S tudy Overview 
This report presents findings from a survey on   the
resignation of the Quebec Premier, François Legault , 
using January data about Québécois ’ attitudes toward 
the CAQ, the Parti Québécois, Quebec Sovereignty, and
vote intentions.

Key Findings 
4 
1 
The public mood toward the CAQ is bleak . 
71% of Quebecers say it’s time for a change.   6-in-10 are dissatisfied with the Quebec government and   48% say that the 
CAQ governments have worsened Quebec's economy. Fran ç ois   Legault never recovered from his late 2022 drop in 
favourability.   Overall net impression of PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is at +9 points, but lower than July 2024 peak
(+20pts). 
2 
Only 22% would vote for the CAQ   if they selected a new leader that implements the changes they want. 
Addressing healthcare issues (14%) and tackling the cost of living (11%) are the top changes people want to see from the
new leader of the CAQ. Only 22% of Quebecers would vote for the CAQ if desired changes are implemented, and   3-in-10
agree with forgiving their mistakes and considering voting for them , with those aged 55+ and those living in the 450 more
likely to forgive the CAQ. 
3 
More Quebecers oppose Quebec sovereignty than support it , and the gap has widened since 2024 . 
Net support for Quebec sovereignty has receded   16 points since June 2024 and stood at -27pts in January 2026 . Most
agree that a PQ government would make the referendum a priority and that it would be a distraction from critical issues,
especially among CAQ and Liberal partisans but even among P Q supporters (31%) . Yet, more than a third of Quebecers and
half of CAQ partisans think the PQ would step back from its commitment to hold a referendum if elected. 
4 
The Parti Quebecois is the frontrunner, with a 5-point lead in decided vote over the Liberals. 
The PQ leads with 31% of decided voters, followed by Liberals at 26% .   Men and francophones are more likely to vote PQ, 
while those 55+ and those living in Quebec City & Chaudière-Appalaches are more likely to vote for the CAQ than average.
Economic Strugglers are more likely to vote PQ, while Achievers are more likely to vote CAQ than average.   The CAQ is in
fourth place with 14%, behind the Conservatives (18%).

Economic Gap 
The economic gap segmentation divides Qu ébécois   by
their outlook on their economic future, splitting them 
into four groups: 
1.   Achievers   (21%) -   Optimistic Qu ébécois   who believe hard work
still leads to success. 
2.   Strugglers   (41%) -   Believe hard work still leads to success but
find it increasingly difficult to get ahead. 
3.   Ambivalent   (22%) -   Uncertain about whether opportunity 
exists or if hard work pays off anymore. 
4.   Alienated   (17%) -   Don’t believe   hard work leads to success 
and feel the system doesn’t work. 
Time For Change 
This segmentation separates Qu ébécois   by their views
on the incumbent government. Is it time for a change, 
and is there a better alternative than the current 
government? This creates six groups: 
1.   Core CAQ   (7%)   -   Strongly support the CAQ and don’t want change. 
2.   Soft CAQ   (8%) -   Lean toward CAQ   but aren’t firmly committed. 
3.   Time for Change CAQ   (10%) -   Want change but still see the CAQ 
as the best option to govern. 
4.   Uncertain   (12%) -   Conflicted about whether it’s time for a change 
at all 
5.   Soft anti-CAQ   (37%) -   Want change and don’t see   the CAQ as the
best government option 
6.   Hostile   (26%)   - Strongly oppose the CAQ and are eager for change 
Key Segmentations:   We use attitudinal clusters to explore opinions within groups that share
common motivations. Detailed definitions and results for each segment are included in the appendix.

Methodology

These are the results of an online survey conducted
between   January 16, 2026, and February 1, 2026 . 
Method:   This online survey was conducted using INNOVATIVE’s Canada 20/20 
national research panel with additional respondents from Lucid, a leading
provider of online samples. Each survey is administered to a series of
randomly selected samples from the panel and weighted to ensure that the 
overall sample’s composition reflects that of the actual Canadian population 
according to Census data to provide results that are intended to approximate
a probability sample. 
Sample Size:   n=   651 Quebec citizens, 18 years or older. The results are 
nationally weighted to n=600 based on Census data from Statistics Canada. 
Field Dates:   January 16, 2026, to February 1, 2026 
Weighting:   Results for Quebec are weighted by age, gender, region, language,
education, and self-reported federal past vote to ensure that the overall 
sample’s composition reflects that of the actual population according to 
Census data. Weighted and unweighted frequencies are reported in the table. 
Margin of Error:   This is a representative sample. However, since the online 
survey was not a random probability-based sample, a margin of error cannot
be calculated. Statements about margins of sampling error or population
estimates do not apply to most online panels. 
Note :   Graphs may not always total 100% due to rounding values rather than
any error in data. Sums are added before rounding numbers.
